docs.title: National Volcano Model
docs.text: The National Volcano Model (NVM) is a framework for understanding volcanic hazard, impact, and risk across Aotearoa New Zealand. It is designed to provide consistent, decision-relevant information that supports planning, preparedness, and resilience across multiple sectors and scales.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Volcanic eruptions can affect communities, infrastructure, and economies across wide areas, often in complex and interconnected ways. However, information about volcanic hazards and their consequences is typically fragmented, difficult to compare, or not directly aligned with decision-making needs.

The NVM addresses this gap by providing a nationally consistent approach to modelling volcanic hazard and translating it into potential impacts and risks. Its purpose is to support:

  • Emergency management and response planning
  • Infrastructure and lifeline resilience planning
  • Government decision-making and policy development
  • Strategic risk assessment at regional and national scales

docs.title: What the model does
docs.text:
The NVM integrates multiple components of risk modelling into a single framework:

  • Hazard — representation of volcanic processes (e.g., ashfall) and their spatial extent and intensity
  • Exposure — the assets, systems, and populations that may be affected
  • Vulnerability — relationships between hazard intensity and expected consequences
  • Risk — the combination of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability to estimate potential impacts

By linking these components, the model moves beyond describing hazards to estimating what those hazards mean in practice.

docs.title: Key principles
docs.text: The development of the NVM is guided by several core principles:

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text: A common modelling framework is used across New Zealand, allowing results to be compared between regions, hazards, and scenarios.

docs.title: Decision relevance
docs.text: Outputs are designed to support real-world decisions, rather than purely academic analysis.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text: The framework can operate at multiple spatial scales, from local case studies to national assessments.

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text: The model is designed to evolve over time, incorporating additional hazards, assets, and modelling approaches.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The current implementation of the NVM focuses primarily on volcanic ashfall impacts on buildings, using probabilistic hazard modelling, national building exposure information, and vulnerability relationships to estimate damage and loss.

The first technical implementation is documented in:

Hayes, J.L.; Williams, J.H.; Magill, C.R.; O'Leary, T.M.; Bebbington, M.; Wilson, T.M.; Leonard, G.S.; Fitzgerald, R.H.; Craig, H.; Lindsay, J. 2026. National Volcano Model: Probabilistic volcanic ash building damage. GNS Science report 2026/21. DOI: 10.21420/NSEH-1881.

This ashfall-focused component brings together:

  • Probabilistic eruption occurrence and magnitude information
  • Ashfall hazard modelling using Tephra2
  • A national building exposure dataset
  • New Zealand-specific building vulnerability models developed through structured expert elicitation
  • Probabilistic estimates of building damage, repair cost, average annual loss, and loss exceedance probability

This provides a foundational capability that can be expanded to include:

  • Additional hazards, including volcanic mass-flow hazards such as pyroclastic density currents, lahars, and lava flows
  • Infrastructure systems (e.g., transport, power, water)
  • Broader societal impacts and disruption

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
New Zealand has multiple active volcanic systems capable of producing widespread impacts. Understanding these impacts in a consistent and comparable way is essential for:

  • Identifying areas of higher risk
  • Prioritising resilience investments
  • Supporting coordinated planning across sectors
  • Improving preparedness for large-scale events

The NVM provides a step toward a more integrated, national-scale understanding of volcanic risk.

docs.title: How to use this documentation
docs.text:
This documentation provides an overview of the structure, components, and outputs of the model.

  • The Model Components section details hazard, vulnerability, and risk
  • The Outputs section explains what the model produces
  • The Guidance section outlines how results should be interpreted

docs.title: Hazard
docs.text:
The hazard component describes the volcanic processes that may affect exposed assets. In the current NVM implementation, the primary hazard is volcanic ashfall from New Zealand volcanoes.

There are three critical components to hazard:

  • Probability
  • Hazard Intensity
  • Spatial extent

For volcanic ashfall, the hazard intensity measure is commonly represented using ash thickness or loading. These measures are important because they can be related to building damage mechanisms such as roof loading, ash ingress, abrasion, corrosion, and cleanup requirements.

docs.title: Probabilistic
docs.text:
The NVM uses a probabilistic approach rather than a single deterministic eruption scenario. This means the model represents many possible volcanic futures, including uncertainty in eruption occurrence, eruption magnitude, wind conditions, ash dispersal, and resulting ashfall footprints.

In the ashfall building damage report, probabilistic eruption occurrence and magnitude information is combined with ashfall hazard modelling to estimate the likelihood of ashfall intensities at locations across New Zealand. This supports outputs such as:

  • Spatial variation in ashfall risk
  • Contributions from different volcanic sources
  • Loss exceedance probabilities
  • Average annual loss estimates

The probabilistic framing allows results to be compared consistently across regions and volcanic sources, while keeping uncertainty explicit.

docs.title: Multi-hazard eruption scenarios
docs.text:
The current national implementation focuses on ashfall building damage. However, volcanic eruptions can produce multiple hazards, including ashfall, pyroclastic density currents, lahars, lava flows, debris flows, ballistic projectiles, and gas emissions.

The NVM is designed to evolve toward multi-hazard volcanic risk assessment. The 2026 report notes that fragility functions were also developed for building damage from volcanic mass-flow hazards, although these were not applied in the ashfall-focused national loss analysis. These functions provide a starting point for future model components that represent hazards beyond ashfall.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: The NVM produces decision-focused outputs that summarise volcanic impact and risk. In the current ashfall building damage implementation, outputs focus on damage and financial loss to buildings.

docs.title: Current ashfall building outputs
docs.text:
The current model produces:

  • Building damage state probabilities
  • Repair cost estimates
  • Average annual loss
  • Loss exceedance probabilities
  • Maps of spatial variation in risk
  • Summary graphs and tables
  • Comparisons of volcanic-source, regional, and building-component contributions to risk

docs.title: Damage states
docs.text: Damage states describe the severity of expected physical consequences for buildings. They provide a practical bridge between hazard intensity and the kinds of impacts that matter for response, recovery, repair, and financial loss estimation.

docs.title: Financial loss
docs.text: Financial loss outputs translate expected building damage into repair costs and other loss metrics. These outputs help compare risk across regions, building types, and volcanic sources in a consistent way.

docs.title: Maps and summaries
docs.text: Spatial outputs show how risk varies across New Zealand. Summary outputs can be used to compare regions, identify important contributors to national risk, and communicate model results to decision-makers.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Outputs are probabilistic and should not be read as predictions of what will happen in a specific eruption. They are designed for comparing risk, testing assumptions, supporting planning, and identifying where more detailed analysis may be needed.

docs.title: Impact/Risk
docs.text: Impact and risk models combine hazard, exposure, and vulnerability.

docs.title: Framework
docs.text:
Risk = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability

Within the NVM, these components are interpreted as:

  • Hazard: the probability, intensity, and spatial footprint of volcanic hazards such as ashfall
  • Exposure: the buildings, infrastructure, land uses, or other assets located in places that may be affected
  • Vulnerability: the expected response of those assets when exposed to a given hazard intensity

The current ashfall building implementation combines probabilistic ashfall hazard, national building exposure, and New Zealand-specific building vulnerability models to estimate damage and financial loss.

docs.title: Ashfall building damage and loss
docs.text:
The 2026 NVM report presents the first national probabilistic assessment of volcanic ash risk to New Zealand buildings. The model estimates risk by running ashfall hazard information through building vulnerability relationships and loss calculations.

Key risk metrics include:

  • Damage probabilities for representative building types
  • Repair cost estimates
  • Average annual loss
  • Loss exceedance probabilities
  • Regional and volcanic-source contributions to national risk

These outputs are intended to support consistent comparison across regions and volcanic sources. They are most useful for strategic planning, resilience investment, emergency management preparedness, and financial risk assessment.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text:
Uncertainty is a central part of the NVM framework. It arises from hazard modelling, eruption occurrence and magnitude assumptions, building exposure information, vulnerability relationships, and loss modelling assumptions.

The current implementation explicitly incorporates uncertainty in building response through expert elicitation and calibrated aggregation. Results should therefore be interpreted as probabilistic estimates rather than precise predictions for a future eruption.

docs.title: Guidance
docs.text: Outputs should be interpreted carefully. The NVM is designed to support planning, comparison, and decision-making, not to provide exact predictions for a specific future eruption.

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
• Uncertainty in eruption occurrence, eruption magnitude, wind conditions, and ash dispersal
  • Uncertainty in building exposure information and replacement or repair costs
  • Uncertainty in vulnerability relationships and expert-derived damage estimates
  • Limitations of modelling ashfall separately from other volcanic hazards
  • Differences between national-scale modelling and local site-specific assessment

docs.title: Appropriate uses
docs.text:
The current ashfall building outputs are most appropriate for:

  • Comparing volcanic ashfall building risk across regions
  • Understanding relative contributions from different volcanic sources
  • Supporting strategic resilience planning
  • Informing emergency management preparedness
  • Exploring sensitivity to vulnerability and loss assumptions

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The current implementation focuses on volcanic ashfall impacts to buildings. It does not yet provide a complete multi-hazard volcanic risk assessment, and it does not directly model infrastructure disruption, agricultural losses, life safety, or wider social and economic impacts.

Results should be treated as nationally consistent risk estimates. For project design, engineering assessment, emergency response operations, or local planning decisions, NVM outputs should be used alongside local data, expert judgement, and other relevant hazard and impact information.

docs.title: Source report
docs.text:
The current ashfall building damage component is documented in:

Hayes, J.L.; Williams, J.H.; Magill, C.R.; O'Leary, T.M.; Bebbington, M.; Wilson, T.M.; Leonard, G.S.; Fitzgerald, R.H.; Craig, H.; Lindsay, J. 2026. National Volcano Model: Probabilistic volcanic ash building damage. GNS Science report 2026/21. DOI: 10.21420/NSEH-1881.

docs.title: Vulnerability models
docs.text:
Vulnerability provides the connection to translate hazard intensity into consequences for assets.

In the NVM, vulnerability models describe how exposed assets are expected to respond when affected by volcanic hazards. For buildings, this response may be expressed as damage states, probabilities of reaching those states, repair costs, or loss ratios.

docs.title: Buildings
docs.text:
The current NVM implementation focuses on New Zealand buildings exposed to volcanic ashfall. The 2026 technical report develops New Zealand-specific vulnerability models for representative building typologies using structured expert elicitation.

These vulnerability models support estimates of:

  • Probability of reaching defined building damage states
  • Expected repair costs
  • Building component contributions to loss
  • Uncertainty in damage and loss estimates

Expert judgement was calibrated and aggregated using Cooke's Classical Model. This provides a formal way to combine expert estimates while accounting for uncertainty and expert performance on calibration questions.

docs.title: Fragility functions
docs.text: Fragility functions estimate the probability that a building reaches or exceeds a specified damage state for a given hazard intensity. In the ashfall component, these functions link ashfall intensity to likely building damage.

docs.title: Vulnerability and loss
docs.text: Vulnerability relationships translate physical damage into financial consequences. In the NVM ashfall component, damage estimates are connected to repair costs and loss metrics so that results can be interpreted in terms of risk to the built environment.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text: Infrastructure vulnerability is not yet part of the current national ashfall building loss implementation. Future versions of the NVM may include transport, power, water, telecommunications, and other lifeline infrastructure as exposure and vulnerability data become available.

docs.title: Agriculture
docs.text: Agricultural impacts are outside the current ashfall building damage implementation. Future extensions may include primary production, rural land use, and sector-specific disruption where suitable vulnerability models and exposure datasets are available.

docs.title: Life safety
docs.text: Life safety is not currently modelled as a direct NVM output. The present implementation focuses on building damage and financial loss from volcanic ashfall. Life safety considerations may require different exposure data, occupancy assumptions, warning and evacuation assumptions, and vulnerability models.
